opus-5.5.text:
I think Leo's ability to recognize talent is one of the most underrated parts of what makes a great advisor. People usually focus on an advisor's own research, but a lot of Leo's impact comes from choosing people and then giving them the right kind of space.

What struck me most is that Leo doesn't look only at a polished résumé or a list of publications. Leo pays attention to how a student thinks: whether you can ask a good question, whether you have your own taste, and whether you're willing to stay with a hard problem when it isn't working yet. In conversations, Leo would often push on why you found something interesting rather than just what you had done. That tells you a lot about a person's potential.

Leo also has a very broad view of what "talent" looks like. The lab brought together people with very different backgrounds: some strong in math and geometry, some more on the systems or engineering side, some coming from vision or graphics, and later many moving into robotics and embodied AI. Leo seemed to believe that if you put curious, capable people with different strengths together, interesting directions would emerge. Looking back, many of those students went on to open up their own areas, which I think validates that judgment.

The other side of recognizing talent is knowing how to let it grow. Leo wasn't the kind of advisor who hands you a fixed project and tells you exactly what to do. There was a lot of trust and freedom. At first that can feel a bit uncomfortable, because you have to find your own direction. But that process is exactly what turns a student into an independent researcher. When you were really onto something, though, Leo would notice quickly and support you strongly, with resources, collaborators, and encouragement to think bigger.

For me personally, that experience shaped how I try to work with my own students now. I try to look beyond surface credentials, pay attention to curiosity and research taste, and give people room to find the problems they truly care about. I don't think I'm as good at it as Leo yet, but it's something I'm consciously learning from.

r001.rationale: The response says Leo looked beyond résumés and publications and paid attention to students’ thinking, but it does not say he judged potential solely through his own observation.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think that's one of the most underrated things about him. People talk about Leo's own research, his taste in problems, but what struck me over the years was how good he was at seeing something in people before they could see it in themselves.

When I joined the lab, I wasn't the obvious pick. My background was a bit off-center, my coursework wasn't the strongest in the cohort, and I remember being quite insecure about that. But he didn't seem to care much about the resume. What he paid attention to was how you reacted when you were confused. Did you get defensive, or did you get curious? Did you keep poking at a thing nobody had asked you to poke at? He told me once that he looks for people who can't help themselves, who will keep working on a problem on a Saturday because it's bothering them, not because anyone is checking.

And he was patient in a way that I only appreciated later. He would give someone a slightly open-ended problem, not a fully specified one, and just watch what they did with it. Some people froze, some people narrowed it down into something safe, and a few people would come back with a question he hadn't thought of. Those were the ones he invested in. He didn't need you to be good yet. He needed to see the shape of what you could become.

Looking back at the people who came out of his group, the pattern is striking. Many of them weren't stars when they arrived, but they became very independent researchers. I think that's partly selection and partly how he treated you once you were there. He gave you more rope than you probably deserved, and most people grew into it.

So I'd say his eye for talent wasn't magic. It was that he was looking at different signals than most advisors, and he was willing to bet on them early.

r001.rationale: The response describes Leo personally observing how people handled open-ended problems and reacted to confusion, but it does not say his judgment relied solely on his own observation.

That’s the lens I’d use to assess Leo’s judgment, but I’d hesitate to make a stronger claim without a concrete example.

sol-6.1.text: I think the real test is whether an advisor can recognize potential before someone has an impressive publication record. Can they see how a student thinks, what questions they ask, and how they respond when an idea doesn’t work? That’s what I’d focus on in judging Leo’s ability to recognize research talent. And I’d give equal weight to what happens afterward—recognizing potential and helping someone develop it are closely connected.
